did_you_know.text: Psalm 131 opens with the heading “A Song of Ascents, of David,” as it appears in the text of the psalm itself.
The speaker describes humility through three parallel negatives: “My heart is not proud,” “my eyes are not haughty,” and “I do not concern myself with great matters or things too wonderful for me.”
The phrase “I do not concern myself with great matters or things too wonderful for me” expresses the recognition that some things are beyond the speaker’s understanding or ability.
The verse says, “I have calmed and quieted my soul”—a description of a soul that has become peaceful and serene.
The verse compares the soul to “a weaned child with its mother,” meaning a child who has been weaned and remains close to its mother; the image conveys calm and closeness.
The repetition of the word “weaned” reinforces the central image of a child resting securely beside its mother.
At the end of the psalm, the focus shifts from the individual to the community: after describing the speaker’s humility, he addresses Israel and calls on it to “hope in the Lord.”
Israel’s hope is directed toward the Lord “from now and forever,” an expression emphasizing its continuance through all time.
